title: Hamlet Builds a Threat-Hunting Program at Denmark Cyber Defense
context_md:
Hamlet, Threat Hunter at *Denmark Cyber Defense*, has been promoted to lead the firm's newly chartered detection-engineering and hunting program. The catalyst was an eleven-night insider incident he identified last quarter through behavioral anomaly scoring — an event that none of the standing detection rules had triggered on. The board read his post-incident write-up and decided the SOC needed to operate proactively, not just reactively.

Hamlet inherits a SIEM that ingests roughly 14 billion events per day from endpoints, firewalls, identity, cloud, and email — but whose detection rules were largely copied from the original vendor templates and have not been measured for false-positive rate in years. The SOC analyst queue receives over 500 alerts per shift, most of which get acknowledged without investigation because the analysts simply do not have time. Threat intelligence is being collected from three commercial feeds, two ISAC memberships, and CISA's automated indicator-sharing program, but indicators are being applied directly to the perimeter firewall blocklist with no scoring or aging — and last month a major SaaS provider's IP range got blocked for six hours because of a stale entry.

Hamlet's six-month plan must rebuild the data pipeline, modernize detection, formalize threat hunting, and bring threat-intelligence consumption under control.

prompt_md: Map each scorecard row to Hamlet's program control, then click **Check answers**.
body_md:
The *SIEM ingestion* row is fixed at the foundation. Hamlet standardizes the **{{schema}}** stage on OCSF so that authentication events from Active Directory, EDR process telemetry, and cloud audit logs can be joined on common user, host, and IP fields.

The *Storage architecture* row is fixed by reorganizing into **{{tiers}}** — fast SSD for the last fourteen days where active investigation happens, object storage for the rest of the year, and cold archive beyond that.

The *Detection engineering* row is fixed by adopting a **{{daa}}** workflow in which every rule lives in a Git repository, is reviewed like application code, is tested in staging against historical data, and has its false-positive rate measured weekly. He commits to the open vendor-neutral rule format **{{rulelang}}** so that the team can both consume community rules from SigmaHQ and contribute back.

To close the gap captured in the *Anomaly detection* row, Hamlet deploys a **{{ueba}}** platform that builds per-user and per-entity baselines and surfaces statistical deviations the static rules would never have anticipated. Particularly powerful is its **{{peer}}** capability, which compares a finance analyst's access patterns against other finance analysts — surfacing access that is technically authorized but anomalous for the role.

Hamlet formalizes threat hunting as a structured, **{{hypothesis}}**-driven activity. Each hunt begins with a specific testable claim about how an adversary would behave, draws on existing telemetry, and ends with one of three outcomes: an incident, a new detection rule that operationalizes what was learned, or documented evidence of coverage. To increase signal where the noise is highest, the team also deploys cheap decoy secrets — **{{tokens}}** — in fileshares, developer home directories, and password vaults so that any interaction at all generates a high-confidence alert.

The *Threat-intel pipeline* row is fixed by inserting a **{{tip}}** between the external feeds and any enforcement point. It deduplicates indicators across feeds, ages them based on first-seen and last-seen dates, scores them by source fidelity, and enriches SIEM alerts with adversary context. Indicators flow downstream to the firewall, DNS resolver, and EDR through the platform's policy — never directly from the raw feed. The data model used to describe each indicator and its relationships to TTPs and campaigns is **{{stix}}**, and the transport that carries those bundles between the platform and external partners is **{{taxii}}**.

The *Executive reporting* row's vanity headline is replaced on the dashboard with two outcome-oriented numbers: **{{mttd}}** (the average time from initial compromise to detection) and the average time from detection to containment.

schema.explanation: Normalizing raw logs into a consistent schema — OCSF or ECS — at ingest is what makes cross-source correlation possible. Without it, joining an AD authentication to an EDR process is impractical at scale.

distractors: a single hot index for everything
tiers.explanation: Tiered storage balances query latency against retention cost: recent days on fast indexed storage, months on object storage, archive for long-tail compliance retention.

daa.explanation: Treating detections as code — Git-managed, peer-reviewed, tested in staging, FPR-measured — is the standard rigor for modern detection engineering.

rulelang.explanation: Sigma is the vendor-neutral YAML SIEM rule format with converters into specific SIEM query languages (Splunk SPL, KQL, ES|QL). YARA is for file content; Snort/Suricata are for network packets.

ueba.explanation: User and Entity Behavior Analytics build per-entity baselines from historical telemetry and surface statistical deviations — the right tool for the compromised-credential, insider, and post-compromise lateral-movement classes of threat.

peer.explanation: Peer-group analysis compares an entity against others in the same role to surface deviations that do not violate explicit access-control rules — a hallmark UEBA primitive.

hypothesis.explanation: Threat hunting is hypothesis-driven by definition. A useful hunt starts with a specific testable claim about adversary behavior, draws on existing telemetry, and produces an artifact regardless of outcome.

tokens.explanation: Honey tokens are decoy secrets placed in legitimate-looking locations whose use generates a high-confidence alert — signal-to-noise approaches one because no legitimate user has any reason to use them.

tip.explanation: A TIP (MISP, Anomali, ThreatConnect, ThreatQuotient) deduplicates indicators across feeds, ages them, scores them by fidelity, and feeds curated indicators to enforcement points — the missing layer in Denmark Cyber Defense's old setup.

stix.explanation: STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression) is the JSON data model for threat intelligence — indicators, malware, campaigns, threat actors, TTPs, sightings.

taxii.explanation: TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information) is the HTTPS REST transport protocol that carries STIX bundles between TIPs, ISACs, and vendors. STIX is the data; TAXII is the pipe.

mttd.explanation: MTTD measures how long an intrusion dwells before discovery — the canonical detective-effectiveness metric, and the right replacement for vanity volume metrics like events processed per day.
